physical_harm: 98% burn injuries leading to death of the wife and stillborn child
number_of_offences: Two offences charged (Sections 302 and 316 IPC), both upheld
premeditation_planning: Not premeditated, but a result of sudden fight and quarrel in the heat of passion
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the prosecution's evidence that the appellant poured kerosene on his wife, leading to burn injuries and her death, as well as the fact that the deceased gave birth to a stillborn child. The court also relied on the testimony of the maternal grandmother (PW-7) and maternal aunt (PW-8) of the deceased, who witnessed the incident and corroborated the deceased's dying declaration.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses, PW-7 and PW-8, as credible, noting that their statements were consistent with the deceased's dying declaration and that they were present at the scene. The court also acknowledged that although PW-1 (the magistrate who recorded the dying declaration) was declared hostile due to discrepancies, there was still sufficient evidence to support the prosecution's case.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 26.01.2007; Trial judgment: Not stated; High Court decision: 23.11.2010; Supreme Court decision: 01 February 2024
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Sudhanshu S. Choudhari, Ms. Rucha Pande, M Veera Ragavan, Ms. Gautami Yadav, Pranjal Chapalgaonkar, M. A. Chinnasamy, Advs. Counsel for the State: Bharat Bagla, Siddharth Dharmadhikari, Aaditya Aniruddha Pande, Sourav Singh, Aditya Krishna, Ms. Raavi Sharma, Adarsh Dubey, Advs.
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted under Sections 302 and 316 IPC; High Court: Upheld conviction; Supreme Court: Appeal partly allowed, conviction converted to Section 304 Part II IPC
prosecution_argument: The prosecution has been able to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt regarding the incident. The maternal grandmother of the deceased witnessed the incident, and she along with the maternal aunt clearly established the facts. Even though PW 1 who recorded the dying declaration was declared hostile, there is sufficient evidence to prove that it was the appellant who had poured kerosene on the deceased which led to the burn injuries and the death of the deceased and the child she was bearing.
defence_argument: The appellant denies all instances of quarreling with his wife and committing the act as alleged by the prosecution. He also claims that he did not produce any defence witnesses to support his case.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that culpable homicide is not murder if it is committed without premeditation in a sudden fight in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel and without the offender’s having taken undue advantage or acted in a cruel or unusual manner.
precedent_relied_upon: Kalu Ram v. State of Rajasthan, (2000) 10 SCC 324
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the act of the appellant was not premeditated but a result of sudden fight and quarrel in the heat of passion. Therefore, the findings of Section 302 were converted to that of Section 304 Part II, and the accused was sentenced to 10 years of R.I.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The act was not premeditated, but a result of sudden fight and quarrel in the heat of passion. The appellant had knowledge of the consequences of his act but no intention to cause death.
other_sentence_order: The appellant was directed to pay fine amount of Rs.5000 and Rs.2000/-, respectively. Since the appellant has already undergone incarceration for more than 10 years, he shall be released forthwith from the jail unless required in some other offence.
